content.text: Hello! Welcome to the final lesson of the Trees & BST module. Today, we will solve an advanced and interesting problem: **Merge Two BSTs**. Given two Binary Search Trees, how do we merge them into a single, height-balanced BST? We'll combine our knowledge of traversals, merging, and tree building to solve this. Let's do it!

Instead of inserting elements from one tree into another one by one (which would be slow and might make the tree unbalanced), we use a highly optimized 3-step strategy:
1. **Flatten to Sorted Lists**: Perform Inorder traversal on both BSTs to extract their elements into two separate sorted arrays. (Time: $O(N_1 + N_2)$).
2. **Merge Sorted Lists**: Combine these two sorted arrays into one single sorted array using the two-pointer merge algorithm from Merge Sort. (Time: $O(N_1 + N_2)$).
3. **Build Balanced BST**: Convert the final sorted array into a height-balanced BST by recursively picking the middle element as the root node. (Time: $O(N_1 + N_2)$).
Here is the C++ implementation, demonstrating the 3 steps working together:

· **Time Complexity**: **$O(N_1 + N_2)$** where $N_1$ and $N_2$ are the number of nodes in tree 1 and tree 2. Every node is visited a constant number of times.
· **Space Complexity**: **$O(N_1 + N_2)$** auxiliary space to store the flattened node values in arrays.

Why is pick-the-middle-element logic used when building a balanced BST from a sorted array?
options: To ensure all elements are even numbers.
It splits the elements evenly, ensuring the height of left and right subtrees remains balanced.
To discard half of the elements.

content.text: To wrap up: We merge two BSTs efficiently in $O(N_1 + N_2)$ time by converting them to sorted lists, merging them, and rebuilding a balanced BST from the middle outward. Congratulations on completing the Trees & BST module! Next up: AVL Trees!
